summary: Analyzes the problems of updating IPv6 addresses of hosts in enterprise networks that need static addresses for operational reasons. It is a problem statement and it is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: When an office moves to a new street, some computers need to keep a fixed address written down everywhere. This explains why changing them is hard.

questions: how to renumber ipv6 hosts with static addresses
why do enterprises use static ipv6 addresses
what are the challenges of ipv6 renumbering
subtitle: Why changing IPv6 addresses is hard when they must stay the same

tldr.problem: IPv6 networks sometimes need static addresses for servers, devices and infrastructure, but changing those addresses when the network renumbers is complex and risky.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC analyzes seven distinct operational reasons why static addresses are needed and what happens when each category must be renumbered.
tldr.outcome: Most problems can be solved with proper configuration management, use of names instead of addresses for discovery, and following a gradual renumbering procedure.

today: RFC 6866 remains the definitive analysis of IPv6 static address challenges in enterprise networks. It is not obsoleted and provides guidance that remains relevant as IPv6 deployments mature.

sections.title: Introduction and Scope
sections.content:
This problem statement examines why enterprise networks have hosts with static IPv6 addresses and what challenges arise when those addresses must change. The issue stems from operational practices developed over decades, when IP addresses were always manually assigned and rarely changed. The document focuses on enterprise networks, particularly those with hundreds or thousands of hosts.

A static address is one that an administrator intends to keep constant for years, regardless of restarts or other events. Static addressing usually implies manual configuration, though it can also be done automatically through systems like stateful DHCPv6. The real problem is that static hosts force subnets to have static prefixes, and that creates a ripple of dependencies across the network.
sections.plainLanguage: Offices use static addresses for the same reason your mailbox number doesn't change when the building is renovated: because everything is labeled with that number.

sections.title: Why Static Addresses Are Used
sections.content:
Enterprises keep static addresses for multiple practical reasons. First, some devices like printers are accessed by typing in their address directly on other computers, so the address must not change. Second, servers often have static addresses to avoid DNS caching issues and to make operations simpler. Third, virtual machines need stable addresses during live migration between physical servers. Fourth, large campus networks track desktop computers by binding their MAC address to a fixed IPv6 address for security incident tracking and asset management.

Additionally, some software licensing schemes still depend on IP addresses, network elements like routers and firewalls need static addresses for management systems to monitor them, and Access Control Lists often reference IP addresses directly. Each of these creates a strong operational reason to use static addressing.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine your ISP (internet company) gives you a new phone number because they're upgrading. Now you'd have to tell every friend, bank and doctor about the change. Some offices have hundreds of these numbers written down everywhere.

sections.title: The Renumbering Problem
sections.content:
When a network must change its IPv6 prefix (because it gets a new ISP or reorganizes subnets), every host with a static address must be updated. If the address is configured manually on each host, an administrator must log in to every machine individually, a time-consuming and error-prone task. If the address is served by a configuration system, the database must be updated, and then every affected host must be told to request a new one. Network management systems must be updated with the new addresses. Security ACLs must be rewritten. DNS records and reverse DNS must change.

For servers and other infrastructure, the deprecation period described in RFC 4192 allows old and new prefixes to coexist briefly so that active connections can wind down. But this requires careful planning and coordination across the entire network.
sections.plainLanguage: If you use the same phone number for fifteen years, it gets written in hundreds of places: your website, business cards, family contact lists, school records. Changing it means finding and updating every single place.

sections.title: Specific Challenges by Use Case
sections.content:
For printers and similar servers without DNS names, renumbering means updating every user's computer. For servers with DNS names, automatic centralized configuration makes renumbering manageable, but manual configuration does not. Virtual machines face conflicts between address stability and host migration. Desktop client machines statically addressed for asset management can usually tolerate gradual address deprecation. Network elements need management systems informed when their addresses change, and some require a restart. Software licensing based on addresses may need administrative updates with the licensing vendor.

Each scenario requires a different approach. The document concludes that a unified configuration management system is the best foundation, combined with a policy of using DNS names and discovery protocols instead of hardcoded addresses wherever possible.
sections.plainLanguage: Different things (printers, websites, computers, routers) have different reasons for needing static addresses. A printer that has no name is much harder to change than a website with a proper DNS address.

sections.title: Summary and Recommendations
sections.content:
The document summarizes four key recommendations to minimize renumbering pain. First, use a centralized configuration management database that controls all prefixes, all DHCPv6 settings, all DNS records, and all router configurations in a consistent way. Second, ensure all local servers are accessed via DNS or discovery protocols, never by hardcoded address. Third, use a Unique Local Address (ULA) prefix for internal traffic, so internal renumbering does not disrupt externally visible services. Fourth, use the gradual RFC 4192 procedure for any prefix renumbering to avoid service interruption.

The document identifies remaining open questions: whether loss of extremely long-lived transport sessions is acceptable during renumbering, whether network elements can be renumbered without interrupting user sessions, and whether any software licensing systems require manual intervention.
sections.plainLanguage: The cure is to organize everything with a single master list (a configuration database), use proper names instead of numbers, keep internal numbers separate from external ones, and make changes gradually.
